newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan prosecutors step up Sumitomo case.
newsitem.headline: Japan prosecutors step up Sumitomo case.

text.p: Prosecutors Wednesday arrested Sumitomo Corp.'s former star copper trader for a second time and said his alleged schemes involved deals with some of the financial world's most respected blue-chip firms.
The firms were not accused of any wrongdoing, but the new arrest warrant against ex-trader Yasuo Hamanaka said he was suspected of committing fraud to cover up money-losing deals with them.

Sumitomo, which filed the formal complaints leading to Hamanaka's arrest, has accused him of racking up a $2.6 billion loss from secret trades in what has become the biggest loss ever by any single trader.

Hamanaka was already in custody on forgery charges when he was served the new arrest warrant. Tokyo prosecutors indicted him on four counts of forgery on Tuesday, the crime he was first arrested for on Oct. 22.

A statement by the prosecutors Wednesday said Hamanaka was suspected of fraudulently procuring about $771 million from a Sumitomo Hong Kong subsidiary to cover massive losses from off-the-book copper options deals with Morgan Guaranty Trust Co. of New York.
The statement said he told a finance official at the Hong Kong unit the funds were for the purchase of copper warrants.

With Wednesday's announcement, Morgan Guaranty joins London Metal Exchange broker Credit Lyonnais Rouse and firms from the Merrill Lynch group as those listed by Tokyo prosecutors as counter-parties to Hamanaka's allegedly illicit deals.
Two allegedly forged documents involved copper options deals with Credit Lyonnais Rouse in 1993, which the prosecutor's office said resulted in heavy losses for Hamanaka.
The others authorised him to make deals with a firm in the Merrill Lynch group and to designate individuals who could withdraw funds deposited with the Merrill Lynch group.
Top Sumitomo officials have repeatedly insisted that none of Hamanaka's superiors knew of his allegedly illicit deals, which are also the subject of investigations by U.S. and British regulators.
One of Hamanaka's lawyers said the former trader could face up to 10 years in prison if convicted on the fraud charges, compared with a maximum five-year sentence for forgery.
The lawyer also said that while Hamanaka had admitted committing forgery, he denied manipulating the world copper market or that he acted for personal gain.

Hamanaka was the world's most controversial and influential copper trader until Sumitomo sacked him in June. Traders said that for years, he artificially propped up the price of copper, which is used in a wide variety of products ranging from automobiles to air conditioners.
